response.query: What microarchitectural choices (parallel comparator lanes, Bloom-assisted CAM, two-tier SRAM) best balance lookup latency, area, power, and match accuracy for L_target=10–100 µs on FPGA?
response.answer: For FPGA, two-tier SRAM balances latency, area, power, and accuracy best for lookup times 10–100 µs. SRAM offers lower latency than DDR3 RAM. Parallel comparator lanes can improve match accuracy.

This manuscript critically explores and optimizes the design of a RISC CPU front-end for IoT delivering a two-fold objective: (i) provide an optimized CPU microarchitecture; and (ii) present a set of three design guidelines to steer the implementation of IoT CPUs. The exploration sits on a newly proposed Systems-on-Chip (SoC) and RISC CPU implementing the RISC-V/IMF ISA and accounting for area, timing, and performance design metrics. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first research that analyzes and optimizes the design of FPGA-based load-store RISC CPU considering the combined pros and cons of four microarchitectural components: (i) instruction cache, (ii) on-chip interconnect, (iii) branch prediction schemes and (iv) instruction bus width. results.title: Learn the difference between FPGA and ASIC in 15 minutes - FPGA Technology - FPGAkey
results.content: # Learn the difference between FPGA and ASIC in 15 minutes. What is the difference between FPGA and ASIC? Fruit's A-series processors are typical ASICs. FPGA adopts the concept of LCA (Logic Cell Array), which includes three parts: configurable logic module CLB, output-input module IOB and internal wiring. The complete FPGA design process includes functional description, circuit design and input, functional simulation, synthesis optimization, post-synthesis simulation, implementation and placement and routing, timing simulation, board-level simulation, and verification, debugging, and loading configuration. FPGA and ASIC design flow.jpg. FPGA and ASIC design flow.jpg. In addition, in the ASIC design process, FPGA is often used for prototype verification. FPGA verification is an important part of ASIC design. It can be said that 50-80% of the entire ASIC process is completed by completing FPGA verification. Considering the design cost, FPGA is dominant in small batches, and ASIC is dominant in large batches. With the same process and design, the speed on FPGA should be slower than that on ASIC. Because the FPGA is based on a general structure, that is, LUT (lookup table), it can implement adders, combinational logic, etc., and ASIC, the general adder is the adder, and the comparator is the comparator, the FPGA structure Versatility will inevitably lead to redundancy; in addition, as the basic unit of FPGA is LUT (LUT composes SLICE, SLICE composes CLB-this is the structure of Xilinx), for this large design, if one LUT cannot be realized, two LUTs must be used. Therefore, FPGA is still much larger than ASIC. Under the same process conditions, FPGA is larger than ASIC. FPGAs, especially FPGAs based on look-up tables (LUT) and configuration element technology based on static memory (SRAM) with six transistors per cell and occupy a large amount of silicon area, consume much more power than equivalent ASICs. FPGA is expensive in a single chip, and development tools and risks are basically non-existent. The use of FPGA and ASIC products should be selected according to product positioning and design needs. ASIC can also use a useful skew to increase the speed, which means more methods than FPGA.

results.title: High-level synthesis assisted, low-latency, area- and power-optimized FPGA implementation of MUSIC algorithm for direction-of-arrival estimation - ScienceDirect
results.content: # High-level synthesis assisted, low-latency, area- and power-optimized FPGA implementation of MUSIC algorithm for direction-of-arrival estimation. With a novel high-level synthesis (HLS)-based design approach that optimizes the bit widths for the eigen value decomposition logic, this study presents an area and speed-optimal implementation of MUSIC algorithm on FPGA. The proposed design works in real time to estimate the DOA in less than 1.7 µs (15 % faster than reported values) and uses up to 30 % less resources on the target FPGA compared with other reported implementations. Some of these algorithms rely on array signal processing in the baseband domain [3], [4] to achieve DOA estimation when the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is low—an example is the use of reflected echoes from automotive radars in heavy traffic scenarios or under high electromagnetic disturbance environments [5]. The multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithm was first demonstrated by Schmidt in 1986; its purpose was to achieve high-accuracy DOA estimation for closely spaced targets at the cost of increased algorithm complexity [6]. Essentially, MUSIC is a high resolution direction finding algorithm based on eigen value decomposition of the sensor covariance matrix observed at antenna arrays. tried to simplify the complex signal computations in MUSIC by considering the real and imaginary parts separately and demonstrated that null space of real and imaginary array output covariance matrix coincides with the intersection of the conjugate and original subspaces for noise [10]; this implementation reduced the complexity by 75 % using limited search (only half of the total angular field of view). As discussed in Section 1, many published works are available in the field of “optimized” MUSIC algorithm implementation on the FPGA. This paper proposes a novel FPGA implementation of a MUSIC algorithm for DOA estimation. The implementation works for any SNR greater than 12 dB and can accurately estimate the DOA for two sources in real time on an FPGA. ### FPGA hardware implementation of DOA estimation algorithm employing LU decomposition. * ### High-Resolution Hybrid Hardware Implementation of DOA Estimation Using MVDR and MUSIC Algorithms on RFSoC Gen 3 Platform. * ### An Efficient High-level Synthesis Implementation of the MUSIC DoA Algorithm for FPGA.
